summary.text: An 85-year-old man with visual impairment and no psychiatric history presented to a university hospital centre. He had retinitis pigmentosa with progressive vision loss, tunnel vision in his teenage years, loss of central vision at age 70 and complete blindness at age 80. Visual hallucinations began at age 80, grew more frequent over five years, were usually binocular and pleasant, and he was aware they were unreal. He reported a positive family history of CBS.

Before the EEG he had neurological, neuropsychological and ophthalmologic examinations, and an MRI exam was also performed. Mattis Dementia Rating Scale and MoCA-BLIND scores were 79/79 and 22/22, with cognitive and global functioning considered normal. Examination showed retinal atrophy in both eyes, a decompensated corneal grafting in the left eye, flat flash visual evoked potentials and light perception in both eyes; he underwent a cataract operation of both eyes. The neurologist diagnosed CBS.

High-density EEG lasted about an hour. The first 17 min were an eyes-closed resting state, after which he had vivid visual hallucinations lasting about 20 min, including a huge stone cathedral and an orange shade that changed and darkened. The recording was extremely noisy with massive movement and muscular artifacts, and 7.5 min of resting state and 8 min of hallucination data were kept after artifact rejection.

During hallucinations compared with rest, delta and theta power fell in frontal areas and rose in midline posterior areas, and alpha power rose in occipital areas. Theta connectivity decreased over the whole frontal area and posterior-central areas of the right hemisphere; theta networks showed lower strength and lower local and global efficiency, and higher modularity. Alpha complexity rose over large scalp areas including the midline frontal areas, while delta and theta complexity did not differ.

article_limitations: Single-patient case report of EEG during and without visual hallucinations; the EEG results are scalp-level and the authors state that EEG spatial resolution is low and no compelling evidence for specific brain regions is available.

The left and right hemisphere regions of the alpha-band complexity increase conflict between Results and Discussion and are kept review-only; the undefined label late-onset visual impairment is review-only as an ambiguity against the stated onset of progressive vision loss at age three.

Values printed inside images (figures and the supplementary PDF) are pixel content only; critical t-values from the Figure 3 and Figure 5 captions are review-only because the supplementary images print different thresholds.
The source writes VS where VH is used elsewhere; the printed wording is kept and not corrected.

The MRI exam, gray matter volume and fMRI findings of this patient are cited to an earlier report; only the statements made about this patient in this article are recorded, and the MRI result is not available here.

EEG acquisition settings (hardware, reference, impedance, sampling rate, software), preprocessing and data-handling parameters (analyzed and discarded durations, retained channels, epoch counts, choice of representative electrodes) are methods and are not recorded as patient facts; the recording duration and periods, artifacts, Results-stated retained clean data and critical t-values of this recording are recorded.
